prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

“Let’s be the same wound if we must bleed. Let’s fight side by side, even if the enemy is ourselves: I am yours, you are mine.” —Tommy Olofsson, Sweden I’m not interested in who suffered the most. I’m interested in people getting over it. Once when my father was a boy a stone hit him on the head. Hair would never grow there. Our fingers found the tender spot and its riddle: the boy who has fallen stands up. A bucket of pears in his mother’s doorway welcomes him home. The pears are not crying. Later his friend who threw the stone says he was aiming at a bird. And my father starts growing wings. Each carries a tender spot: something our lives forgot to give us. A man builds a house and says, “I am native now.” A woman speaks to a tree in place of her son. And olives come. A child’s poem says, “I don’t like wars, they end up with monuments.” He’s painting a bird with wings wide enough to cover two roofs at once. Why are we so monumentally slow? Soldiers stalk a pharmacy: big guns, little pills. If you tilt your head just slightly it’s ridiculous. There’s a place in my brain where hate won’t grow. I touch its riddle: wind, and seeds. Something pokes us as we sleep. It’s late but everything comes next.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Let, Tommy, Olofsson

outputs.L1:
“Let’s be the same wound if we must bleed. Let’s fight side by side, even if the enemy is ourselves: I am yours, you are mine.”  
—Tommy Olofsson, Sweden

I’m not interested in who suffered the most. I’m interested in people getting over it.

Once, when my father was a boy, a stone struck him on the head. Hair would never grow there. Our fingers found the tender spot and its riddle: the boy who has fallen stands up. A bucket of pears in his mother’s doorway welcomes him home. The pears are not crying.

Later, his friend who threw the stone says he was aiming at a bird. And my father starts growing wings.

Each of us carries a tender spot: something our lives forgot to give us. A man builds a house and says, “I am native now.” A woman speaks to a tree in place of her son. And olives come.

A child’s poem says, “I don’t like wars; they end up with monuments.” He is painting a bird with wings wide enough to cover two roofs at once.

Why are we so monumentally slow?

Soldiers stalk a pharmacy: big guns, little pills. If you tilt your head just slightly, it’s ridiculous.

There’s a place in my brain where hate won’t grow. I touch its riddle: wind and seeds.

Something pokes us as we sleep. It’s late, but everything comes next.
outputs.L2:
“If blood must be shed, let one injury bind us. We will stand together in battle, even when what we face is within us. I belong to you, and you belong to me.” —Tommy Olofsson, Sweden

I have no desire to measure whose pain was greatest. What matters to me is that people move beyond it.

In childhood, my father was struck in the head by a rock. No hair ever returned to that place. When our fingertips touched the sensitive patch, we encountered its mystery: a fallen boy rises again. At his mother’s entrance, a pail filled with pears receives him. The fruit sheds no tears.

Years afterward, the friend who cast the stone explains that the intended target was a bird. Then wings begin to form on my father.

Everyone bears a vulnerable place—the mark of something life failed to provide.

After constructing a home, a man declares that he now belongs to the land. A woman addresses a tree because her son is absent, and olives appear.

In a poem, a child writes that wars displease him because they conclude in memorials. As he writes, he paints a bird whose outstretched wings can shelter two rooftops simultaneously.

What makes our understanding arrive with such monumental delay?

Armed soldiers prowl around a drugstore: enormous weapons beside tiny medicines. Viewed with your head turned only a little, the scene becomes absurd.

Somewhere in my mind is ground where hatred cannot take root. I press against its mystery and find moving air and scattered seeds.

While we are asleep, something keeps nudging us awake. The hour may be late, yet all that is still to happen lies ahead.
outputs.L3:
The poem urges readers to move beyond comparing suffering or deciding whose pain is greater. Such comparisons only deepen division and prevent genuine understanding. Instead, the poem calls for shared healing, solidarity, and a recognition that suffering, though experienced differently, can create common ground. By acknowledging one another’s wounds with compassion, people can begin to replace isolation and resentment with mutual care.

At the same time, the poem does not suggest that healing is simple. Personal wounds remain tender, especially when important needs have been ignored or forgotten. Yet pain does not have to define the future. Through resilience, vulnerability, and human connection, suffering can be transformed into growth and hope. The poem’s images of home, nature, and belonging reinforce this possibility, suggesting that reconciliation may restore a sense of safety and connection that violence and separation have taken away.

The contrast between children and war makes the poem’s message especially powerful. Children represent innocence, imagination, and the freedom to envision a different world, while war appears absurd, destructive, and tragically enduring. Its monuments preserve memories of conflict, but they also reveal how societies continue to give violence a permanent place in their landscapes and histories. Against this legacy, children embody the possibility of breaking destructive cycles.

Although hatred and conflict persist, the poem ultimately remains hopeful. It affirms that renewal is still possible when people choose compassion over competition, reconciliation over division, and openness over fear. The future cannot erase past suffering, but it can prevent that suffering from becoming the only story. By facing pain honestly while remaining open to change, individuals and communities can recover belonging, rebuild trust, and create the conditions for lasting peace.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores the lasting effects of inherited trauma, war, displacement, and hatred, showing how public conflicts enter the most private areas of human life. Historical violence is not presented as something confined to the past; it survives in memory, family stories, habits, fears, and the sense of belonging—or not belonging—to a place. By approaching these themes through intimate recollections, the poem gives large political events a deeply personal dimension. War becomes more than an abstract struggle between opposing sides: it becomes a wound carried by individuals and passed from one generation to the next.

Surreal imagery allows the poem to express experiences that ordinary language cannot fully contain. Memory, grief, and imagination overlap, blurring the boundaries between past and present. This dreamlike quality reflects the disorientation of displacement and the fragmented nature of trauma. At the same time, the poem places images of tenderness and healing beside images of violence. Small gestures, vulnerable bodies, and symbols of care suggest that human beings retain the capacity for compassion even after enduring profound suffering.

Crucially, the poem refuses to treat hatred as the inevitable outcome of pain. Although wounds can be inherited, vengeance does not have to be. The speaker recognizes suffering without allowing it to become a justification for inflicting suffering on others. In this way, resilience is presented not merely as survival, but as an ethical choice: the decision to resist the cycle in which injury produces resentment and resentment produces further violence.

Imagination plays an important role in making this transformation possible. Through poetry, painful memories can be reshaped into forms that connect people rather than divide them. The wound becomes a source of recognition, allowing one person’s grief to illuminate another’s. Such recognition creates the possibility of solidarity across political, cultural, and historical boundaries. Shared vulnerability becomes more powerful than inherited hostility.

Ultimately, the poem offers a cautious but meaningful hope. It does not deny the reality of conflict or suggest that trauma can be easily erased. Instead, it proposes that people can remember suffering without building their identities around revenge. Rather than endlessly memorializing division, they can turn memory toward empathy, healing, and a renewed sense of common humanity. The poem therefore imagines a future in which wounds are neither forgotten nor worshipped, but transformed into reasons to care for one another.

### Let Tommy Olofsson Inspire a Love of Literature

Let literature open the door to new perspectives. Tommy Olofsson, a Swedish poet, author, translator, and literary critic, has contributed to contemporary Scandinavian culture through his thoughtful engagement with language and poetry. His work reflects a deep interest in how words shape human experience, memory, and imagination.

Through poetry, criticism, and translation, Tommy Olofsson demonstrates how literature can connect people across cultures and generations. His career is a reminder that reading is not simply a pastime—it is a way to explore ideas, emotions, and the complexity of life.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about reconciliation, inherited wounds, and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, using birds, olives, monuments, and childhood memories as recurring imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
At the border, a flock of starlings turns in the evening air, becoming first a hand, then a wound, then a hand again. No one asks the birds for their papers. They cross above the walls and watchtowers, above the stones where names are carved in two languages, above the monuments that insist memory must stand upright even when grief has brought everyone to their knees.

My grandmother kept olives in a blue bowl. Your grandmother kept olives in a green one. Each said the tree in the courtyard had belonged to her father, and to his father before him. Each remembered a childhood ladder leaning into silver leaves, small fingers darkened by the harvest, the taste of salt, the warning not to climb too high. Later, both courtyards existed mainly in stories. Later, the stories grew gates.

We inherit wounds as children inherit lullabies: without choosing the words. A siren enters one dream; a key enters another. There are photographs folded into drawers, uniforms hung behind doors, houses absent from maps but present at every meal. We learn where to place flowers, where to place stones, which monument means deliverance and which means disappearance. We learn to fear the shadow of the other child before we learn the child’s name.

Yet once, before the histories hardened around us, we both chased pigeons through a square. We both believed the birds were playing. We scraped our knees on the same earth and ran crying toward different mothers. Their hands smelled of soap, cumin, tobacco, oranges. Their hands lifted us with the same frightened tenderness.

Reconciliation is not forgetting. It is not pulling down one monument to make room for another. It is standing between them long enough to hear the silence each has buried. It is saying: your dead do not cancel mine. My wound is not healed by deepening yours. The olive tree cannot tell whose sorrow watered it, but it remembers every axe.

At dawn, doves gather on the wall. They are not symbols; they are hungry. Below them, two old men argue over the roots of a tree, then fall quiet when a child reaches for a fallen olive. For a moment, neither asks what the child has inherited. The child turns the bitter fruit in her palm as if it were a small dark planet, as if the world might still be held without being owned.

Above her, the birds rise together—not forgiven, not forgetting, but carried by the same difficult air.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical anti-war poem that begins with a quotation from Swedish poet Tommy Olofsson and ends on a cautiously hopeful note.
counterfactuals.output:
> “En lagom mängd våld”  
> —Tommy Olofsson

As if violence ever learned restraint,  
or fire stopped politely at the door;  
as if the bomb could weigh a child’s sleep  
and choose the empty room.

At dawn, the fields wear ash like snow.  
A cup lies open to the rain.  
Two armies name the same torn river  
theirs, while it carries every name away.

Mothers stitch the dark with whispered songs.  
Fathers search the rubble for a shoe.  
Above them, flags keep arguing with wind,  
bright cloth untouched by blood.

No trumpet tells the whole of grief.  
No map records the cellar’s breath,  
the hand that shares its final crust,  
the stranger lifted through the smoke.

Yet somewhere, beneath the iron weather,  
a seed persists without permission.  
Someone lowers a rifle. Someone listens.  
And morning, wounded, tries again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a free-verse poem arguing that healing matters more than deciding who suffered most, weaving together a father’s childhood injury, a bucket of pears, soldiers outside a pharmacy, and a child painting a bird.
counterfactuals.output:
**No Scale for This**

My father keeps his childhood  
under a pale seam on his knee—  
the day the fence gave way,  
the nail entering like a verdict  
no child had asked to hear.

He tells it softly,  
as if pain were an animal  
that startles when named.

On the table, a bucket of pears  
leans its yellow weight against the afternoon.  
Some are bruised.  
Some ripen without witness.  
We cut away what has darkened,  
eat what is still sweet.

Across town, soldiers stand  
outside the pharmacy,  
rifles crossing their chests  
while the sick wait for doors to open.  
Each person carries a prescription,  
a photograph, a private ruin.  
No one is cured by proving  
their wound the deepest.

In the next room, a child  
paints a bird with three blue wings.  
She has never seen such a creature,  
so she gives it what it needs  
to rise.

Let the historians measure ashes.  
Let the judges number scars.  
But here—bring water,  
bring bandages,  
bring the pears before they spoil.

Ask not whose blood was darker,  
whose night lasted longest.

Ask where it hurts.  
Ask what can be mended.  
Hold still the trembling wing  
until it remembers the sky.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a moving poem about shared trauma and peace in the Middle East, with surreal imagery and the line “There’s a place in my brain where hate won’t grow.”
counterfactuals.output:
At night, the border dreams it is a river,  
forgetting the names of the countries  
that taught it to divide.

A mother in Gaza folds the dark  
around her sleeping child.  
A mother in Tel Aviv wakes  
to the same iron thunder.  
Between them, the moon—  
pale, astonished—  
carries no passport.

The dead walk softly through olive groves,  
their pockets full of keys,  
their mouths full of unfinished songs.  
They sit beneath trees older than sorrow  
and trade photographs of kitchens  
that no longer exist.

There’s a place in my brain where hate won’t grow.  
I guard it like a candle in a shattered house,  
like a seed hidden under the tongue,  
like one clear cup of water  
passed from hand to trembling hand.

One day, the walls may molt their concrete  
and rise as flocks of white birds.  
Sirens may open into lilies.  
The sky may stop mistaking fire  
for a language.

Until then, let grief recognize grief.  
Let every name be spoken as a name,  
not a number, not a weapon.  
Let the wounded earth lie down  
beneath its quilt of stars,

and let us meet there—  
unarmed, unafraid,  
each carrying half of the dawn.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
